I will estimate the causal effect with a lottery-based instrumental-variables design, using random admission offers from oversubscribed charter lotteries as instruments for years enrolled in a charter middle school. The key variables are the treatment (years enrolled in charter), the outcome (standardized 8th-grade state math score), the instruments lottery_offer and, in the second-draw subsample, second_draw_offer, and lottery-cell fixed effects for school, grade, and year. I will run 2SLS with lottery-cell fixed effects, including baseline_math, parent_college, frl, and sibling_charter only to improve precision and check balance. The identifying assumption is that, conditional on lottery cell, the offer affects 8th-grade math only by changing charter enrollment. The main threat is differential attrition or missing test scores, plus potential violations from later charter enrollment outside the lottery, which would limit the estimate to compliers and require attrition/robustness checks. For second_draw_offer, I will analyze it separately among initial non-offer second-draw entrants because it is defined only for that subset.

CANDIDATES:
lottery_offer | plausible
second_draw_offer | plausible
dist_charter | doubtful
sibling_charter | doubtful
parent_college | doubtful
INSTRUMENT: lottery_offer

To avoid the exclusion violation from the district’s May math tutoring of initial-offer holders, I will not use lottery_offer; instead I will restrict to applicants without an initial offer who entered the September second draw and estimate 2SLS of standardized 8th-grade math score on years enrolled in a charter middle school, instrumenting with second_draw_offer. I will include second-draw lottery-cell fixed effects (school-grade-year) and baseline controls (baseline_math, frl, parent_college, sibling_charter, n_ranked, dist_charter). The first stage should show second-draw winners spend about 0.6 more charter years, and the second stage yields the LATE for second-draw compliers. The main threat is that second_draw_offer directly affects math through some non-charter channel; I will test balance on baseline covariates and placebo outcomes to probe this.

I will estimate the effect of years enrolled in a charter middle school on standardized 8th-grade math using a lottery IV design, restricting to applicants without an initial offer who entered the city’s second independent draw and using second_draw_offer as the instrument for charter years, with lottery-cell fixed effects. The key variables are the treatment (years enrolled in a charter school), the outcome (standardized 8th-grade state math score), the instrument (second_draw_offer), baseline_math, and covariates such as parent_college, frl, sibling_charter, and n_ranked. I will fit 2SLS: first stage regresses years enrolled on second_draw_offer plus fixed effects and covariates, and second stage regresses math score on predicted years enrolled plus the same controls, clustering by lottery cell or school. The main threat is exclusion: initial lottery offers are invalid instruments here because initial-offer holders are placed on the district’s confirmed placement roster, which enrolls them in free after-school math tutoring regardless of charter enrollment, while second-draw offers occur after that May roster closes. I will interpret the estimate as a LATE for second-draw entrants/compliers and check first-stage strength and balance on baseline_math and demographics.

I will estimate a two-stage least squares model using second_draw_offer as an instrument for years enrolled in a charter school, restricting to applicants without an initial offer who were entered in the September second draw, with school-grade-year fixed effects to compare students within the same lottery cell. The outcome is the standardized 8th-grade state math score; the endogenous treatment is years enrolled in a charter school; baseline_math, frl, parent_college, sibling_charter, dist_charter, and n_ranked will be included as pre-treatment controls. I will not use lottery_offer because the May tutoring program for all initial-offer holders is a direct effect on math scores independent of charter enrollment, violating the exclusion restriction. The main threat to the second-draw design is that second-draw eligibility is observed only for a selected subset, so the estimated LATE applies to second-draw compliers and may not generalize; additionally, any non-random selection into the second draw or late-offer effects outside charter attendance would threaten exclusion. I will test first-stage strength (0.6 additional years) and report robustness to covariate sets and lottery-cell definitions.

I will estimate the causal effect of years enrolled in a charter middle school on standardized 8th-grade math scores using two-stage least squares in the subsample of applicants without an initial offer who were entered in the city’s second independent lottery draw. The instrument is second_draw_offer, the treatment is years enrolled in a charter school, and the outcome is the standardized 8th-grade state math score, with lottery-cell fixed effects and baseline_math, parent_college, frl, sibling_charter, and n_ranked as covariates. The first stage predicts charter enrollment with second_draw_offer, and the second stage uses predicted enrollment to estimate math-score effects, yielding a local average treatment effect for second-draw compliers. I will not use lottery_offer as an instrument because the district’s May tutoring program for initial-offer holders directly raises math scores even for students who never enroll in a charter, violating the exclusion restriction. The main threat is that second-draw entry may be selective or that second_draw_offer could affect outcomes through non-charter channels; I will check covariate balance, first-stage strength, and robustness. If these diagnostics fail, I will report the estimates as descriptive rather than causal.

The main threat is that second_draw_offer may affect math through non-charter channels, especially differential attrition or unobserved school switching, so I will check balance, first-stage strength, and robustness to missing outcomes. I will report the LATE for second-draw compliers and not extrapolate to all applicants.

I will estimate the causal effect of being inspected in the following year on workers’ compensation injury claims per 100 workers over the next four years using a lottery-based IV/2SLS design, restricting to establishments not drawn in the annual inspection lottery. The endogenous treatment is an indicator for actual agency inspection in the following year, the instrument is followup_draw, the outcome is claims per 100 workers over four years, and I include lottery-stratum fixed effects (industry × region and year) plus baseline covariates such as prior_claims, employees, union, and est_age. I cannot use the annual lottery draw as the instrument because every drawn establishment also received a $5,000 safety-equipment voucher, which can directly reduce injuries and violates the exclusion restriction for inspection. The first stage should show followup_draw raises inspection probability by about 41 percentage points; I will report the first-stage F, balance tests, and reduced-form ITT, and interpret the 2SLS estimate as a LATE for non-drawn compliers. The main threat is that the December lottery’s exclusion restriction could fail if unused inspector hours correlate with unobserved injury determinants or if inspection timing differs, so I will test balance and robustness to strata and covariates.

CANDIDATES:
drawn | violated
followup_draw | plausible
INSTRUMENT: followup_draw

I will estimate the causal effect of an agency inspection in the year after the lottery on workers’ compensation injury claims per 100 workers over the next four years using 2SLS within the sample not drawn in the main inspection lottery, where the December lottery provides exogenous variation in inspection. The instrument is `followup_draw`, which raises inspection probability by 41 percentage points and has no other stated component; the endogenous treatment is actual inspection in the following year from agency records, and the outcome is the four-year injury-claim rate. I will regress inspection on `followup_draw` plus lottery-stratum fixed effects, then regress the injury-claim rate on predicted inspection with the same fixed effects and clustered or robust standard errors. I will not use `drawn` as an instrument because every main-lottery drawn establishment received a separate $5,000 safety-equipment voucher, so its exclusion restriction is violated by a direct safety intervention. The main threat is that this identifies a local average treatment effect for December-lottery compliers among non-main-lottery establishments, so I will check balance, first-stage strength, and sensitivity to stratum definitions and outcome windows.

I will therefore restrict to establishments with `drawn = 0` and use the separate December lottery variable `followup_draw` as the instrument, since it raises inspection probability by 41 percentage points and has no other documented component. The outcome will be workers’ compensation injury claims per 100 workers over the next four years, with industry/region or original lottery-stratum fixed effects and pre-lottery controls included for precision. The main threat is that this identifies a LATE for December-lottery compliers in the non-main-drawn sample, limiting external validity and requiring checks for first-stage strength, balance, and any unrecorded December-lottery side effects.
